source_text: Πολλῷ δὲ τούτου βελτίους οἳ κοινωνίαν ἅμα βίου ἐστείλαντο, ἐξ ἧς καρποῖντο ἂν τὰ βέλτιστα; Δύο γὰρ ἀνδρῶν τοῖς αὐτοῖς πράγμασιν ὀρθῶς προσκειμένων, εἰ καὶ θατέρῳ τινὶ προσπέσῃ τι· ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐ μικρὰν ἐπικουρίαν ἔχει, τὸν αὐτῷ συνόντα. Μεγίστη δὲ καὶ συμφορὰ ἀνθρώπῳ δυσπραγοῦντι, καὶ ἡ ἐρημία τοῦ ἀνακτησομένου. Οἱ δ᾽ αὖ ὁμοδίαιτοι, καὶ τὴν εὐπραγίαν αὐτοῖς ἐδιπλασίασαν, καὶ πραγμάτων ἀβουλήτων χειμῶνα παρεμυθήσαντο· ὥστε καὶ μεθημέραν τῇ ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλοις λαμπρύνεσθαι παρρησίᾳ, καὶ νύκτωρ φαιδρότητι σεμνύνεσθαι. Ὁ δὲ βίον ἀκοινώνητον ἕλκων, φρικώδη τινὰ ἑαυτῷ διεξάγει ζωήν, οὐκ ᾐσθημένος, ὡς εἰ καὶ ἐπίθοιτό τις ἀνθρώποις συμπεφραγμένοις, θρασέως καὶ οὐκ ἀσφαλῶς βουλεύεται, καὶ ὅτι οὐδὲ σχοῖνος τριπλῇ ῥᾳδίως ἀπορρήγνυσθαι πέφυκεν. Ἐγὼ δὲ προκρίνω νέον πένητα σώφρονα, γέροντος βασιλέως ἄφρονος, ᾧ ἐνθύμιον οὐ γεγένηται, ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι, τῶν μὲν ἐκ τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου τινὰ εἰς τὸ βασιλεῦσαι καταστῆναι, αὐτὸν δὲ τῆς ἀδίκου δυναστείας, δικαίως ὕστερον ἐκπεσεῖν. Συμβαίνει γὰρ τοὺς ὑπὸ τῷ νέῳ μέν, ἔμφρονι δὲ τασσομένους, ἀλύπους εἶναι τοὺς ὅσοι προγενέστεροι. Οἱ γὰρ μετέπειτα γενόμενοι, διὰ τὸ ἑτέρου ἀπειράτως ἔχειν, οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἐπαινεῖν δύνανται, ἀγόμενοί τε γνώμῃ ἀλογίστῳ, καὶ ὁρμῇ πνεύματος ἐναντίου. Ἐκκλησιάζων δὲ πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν ἔχε τόν τ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ βίον ὀρθῶς διαπορεύεσθαι, καὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀφρόνων εὔχεσθαι, ὅπως ἐπίσταιντο σύνεσιν λαβόντες, ἐκκλίνειν τὴν πρᾶξιν τῶν πονηρῶν.
thought_title: Two together are helped, the lonely man is exposed
orientation: Gregory continues reporting Solomon's teaching, contrasting shared life with solitary toil and a foolish old king, and ends in his own voice addressing the Church.
pass_a_gloss: But far better than this man are those who have arranged for themselves a partnership of life together, from which would they reap the best things? For when two men rightly devote themselves to the same tasks, even if something should befall the one of the two — yet indeed he has no small help, the one who is with him. And the greatest misfortune for a man faring badly is also the desertedness of one who will raise him up. And those who live together have both doubled their prosperity for themselves and have comforted the winter of unwished-for troubles; so that both by day to be made bright by their openness toward one another, and by night to be adorned with cheerfulness. But he who drags an unshared life leads a certain dreadful life for himself, not having perceived that even if someone should attack men shut together, he deliberates boldly and not safely, and that not even a triple cord is by nature easily broken. But I prefer a young poor prudent man to an old foolish king, to whom it has not become a thought that it is possible for one man from prison to be established to be king, and for himself to fall justly afterwards from his unjust rule. For it happens that those ordered under the young but prudent man, as many as are earlier, are without grief. For those born later, because they hold to another without trial, are not able even to praise this man, being led both by unreasoning judgment and by impulse of a contrary spirit. And addressing the Church, have before your eyes both to pass through your own life rightly and to pray on behalf of the foolish, in order that having received understanding they may know to turn aside from the practice of evil things.

choices.why: keeps κοινωνίαν as shared arrangement, not abstract fellowship, and ἅμα as togetherness

choices.english: the one who is with him
choices.why: literal participle of being-with, preserves helper present beside the fallen man
keeps seasonal metaphor for hardship rather than smoothing to adversity
exact number plus object, matching the proverb image without paraphrase
brief marks this first-person voice as Gregory addressing the Church, not generic preaching

pass_b_english: Far better than that solitary man are those who have made a partnership of life together, for they gather the finest fruit from it (Ecclesiastes 4:9). When two men devote themselves rightly to the same work, if anything happens to one of them, he has great help close by in the one who is with him (Ecclesiastes 4:10). For a man in trouble, the greatest misfortune is to be deserted with no one to raise him up.

Those who live together double their prosperity and comfort one another through the winter of unwelcome troubles. So by day they shine with open confidence in each other, and by night they rest in bright cheer. Whoever drags along an unshared life leads a dreadful life for himself without realizing it: if anyone sets upon people firmly bound together, he schemes boldly but unsafely, for a triple cord is not easily broken (Ecclesiastes 4:12). I myself prefer a poor young man who is wise to a foolish old king (Ecclesiastes 4:13) who has never taken to heart how it can happen that someone rises from prison to become king (Ecclesiastes 4:14), while the king himself justly falls afterward from his unjust rule.

Those who range themselves under the young yet sensible ruler, all who came before, live free from sorrow. But those who come later cannot praise even him, since they have no experience of any other ruler, but are led by thoughtless judgment and the impulse of a contrary spirit. And as you address the Church, keep before your eyes both to guide your own life rightly and to pray for the foolish, that they may gain understanding and learn to turn aside from the practice of evil.

problems.quote: As one addressing the Church, Gregory says keep two things before your eyes
problems.source_quote: Ἐκκλησιάζων δὲ πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν ἔχε τόν τ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ βίον ὀρθῶς διαπορεύεσθαι
problems.why: The Greek is a second-person command to the one addressing the Church, not a narrator reporting that Gregory says it.
problems.fix: And you, as you address the Church, keep before your eyes both to walk your own life rightly and to pray for the foolish
problems.ruling: Source ἔχε is a singular imperative to the preacher (Ἐκκλησιάζων). The English turns it into reported speech by 'Gregory', misstating who is addressed.

edits.old: As one addressing the Church, Gregory says keep two things before your eyes: to guide your own life rightly, and to pray for the foolish,
edits.new: And as you address the Church, keep before your eyes both to guide your own life rightly and to pray for the foolish,

fixed: Fixed speaker: Ἐκκλησιάζων δὲ ... ἔχε is a second-person imperative addressed to the one addressing the Church, so removed third-person 'Gregory says' for direct 'as you address... keep'.

problems.quote: they have no experience of what was before
problems.why: The source says the later people have no experience of another ruler (ἑτέρου). The English changes this to 'what was before', which loses the comparison between rulers.
problems.fix: since they have no experience of any other ruler, they cannot even praise him
problems.ruling: ἑτέρου with τοῦτον means the other man; “what was before” drops that contrast.

edits.old: since they have no experience of what was before
edits.new: since they have no experience of any other ruler

fixed: Fixed 'what was before' -> 'any other ruler': source has ἑτέρου ἀπειράτως ἔχειν (without experience of another), not a reference to earlier time.

problems.quote: someone rises from prison to become king (Ecclesiastes 4:13)
problems.source_quote: τῶν μὲν ἐκ τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου τινὰ εἰς τὸ βασιλεῦσαι καταστῆναι
problems.why: Rising from prison to reign is Ecclesiastes (LXX) 4:14; 4:13 is only the poor youth preferred to the old king.
problems.fix: Cite Ecclesiastes 4:13 for the preference, and Ecclesiastes 4:14 for the rise from prison to the throne.
problems.ruling: The prison-to-king clause (ἐκ τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου… βασιλεῦσαι) is LXX Eccl 4:14, but the English labels it 4:13, so the reference is wrong.

edits.old: who is wise to a foolish old king who has never taken to heart how it can happen that someone rises from prison to become king (Ecclesiastes 4:13)
edits.new: who is wise to a foolish old king (Ecclesiastes 4:13) who has never taken to heart how it can happen that someone rises from prison to become king (Ecclesiastes 4:14)

fixed: wrong_scripture: real — kept 4:13 for the youth-vs-king preference and added 4:14 for τῶν μὲν ἐκ τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου τινὰ εἰς τὸ βασιλεῦσαι καταστῆναι.

refereed.quote: for they gather the finest fruit from it
refereed.source_quote: ἐξ ἧς καρποῖντο ἂν τὰ βέλτιστα;
refereed.why: A potential optative inside a question becomes a flat statement that they do gather the fruit.
refereed.fix: Are those who share life not far better, since from it they might gather what is best?
refereed.ruling: ἐξ ἧς καρποῖντο ἂν τὰ βέλτιστα is optative with ἂν inside a question; English states flatly 'they gather the finest fruit', dropping the question and potential mood.
